(out/'manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(texts))
print(''.join(texts[:3]))

strengths: The paper addresses an important NLP problem: characterizing degrees of human contribution beyond binary AI-text detection. Its explicit distinction between informational contribution and creativity or legal authorship usefully limits the intended construct.

The experiments have substantial breadth: four domains, six generation models, two scoring models, repeated generations, and real-world WildChat examples. The consistent ordering of polishing, summary-based generation, and less informative prompting supports the score’s usefulness for distinguishing broad generation modes.

The human evaluation provides meaningful supporting evidence: three annotators assess 1,500 pairs, with 91.47% unanimous agreement and 95.93% agreement between majority judgments and the input-aware measure on the selected pairs.
The proposed computation is simple, and the appendices provide useful dataset sources, prompt templates, model identifiers, and threshold-calibration details.
weaknesses: The central interpretation as a proportion of human-contributed information is insufficiently justified. Equations 1–5 compute a pointwise log-likelihood ratio, not Shannon mutual information. Interpreting this ratio as pointwise mutual information additionally requires a compatible marginal distribution over outputs; the empty-context model distribution is not shown to be that marginal over human prompts. The normalized score can also be negative even with known input and the exact model whenever p(y|x) < p(y). These issues undermine the shared-information diagram and require more careful interpretation of reported contribution percentages.

The text-only extension establishes a bound conditional on a chosen plausibility criterion, but does not establish the claimed minimum necessary contribution. Equation 10 substitutes the bound for the minimum without demonstrating attainability or tightness. Selecting the conditional-surprisal cutoff as an empirical mean plus one standard deviation does not establish coverage for actual generations across domains. Evaluation should directly measure bound violations and tightness using available input-output pairs; agreement with ordinal human judgments does not validate these properties.

The output-only score is exactly a monotonic transformation of average token surprisal: writing h = I(y)/N and c = -log τ gives φ̂ = 1 - c/h. Consequently, its rankings and ROC–AUC are identical to those of ordinary perplexity under the same scoring model. This relationship should be explicit and situated against likelihood-based detection. The reported detection performance demonstrates discriminative signal, but does not independently substantiate the interpretation as minimum human contribution.

The validation favors coarse distinctions and lacks essential controls. Annotation pairs are selected only when the proposed input-aware score differs by more than 0.1, so the reported agreement excludes cases the method considers difficult and does not establish performance on an independently sampled population. The synthetic conditions also differ substantially in input length and textual overlap. Comparisons against input/output length ratios, lexical overlap, and semantic similarity, together with independently selected and within-condition comparisons, are needed to establish what the proposed measure adds. Distributional ordering alone does not establish calibrated percentages.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the helpful appendix. The manuscript provides no release link for the constructed generations, annotations, or implementation, and does not adequately specify chat serialization, empty-context scoring, special-token handling, or whether scoring probabilities incorporate generation temperature. These choices directly affect both likelihood-based measures. Clarifying the central interpretation, strengthening independent validation, and documenting the scoring implementation are important revisions needed before a sound Findings recommendation.
